chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Abdullah ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Isa al-Qummi, who said:
I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): 'I shoot my arrow and I do not know whether I named (said bismillah) or did not name.' He said: 'Eat — there is no problem.'
He (the narrator) said: I said: 'I shoot and it disappears from me, then I find my arrow in it.' He said: 'Eat what has not been eaten from it, but if it had been eaten from, do not eat from it.'

key_terms.سَمَّى: To name/invoke — reciting 'Bismillah' at the time of releasing a hunting implement, a required condition for the permissibility of hunt
key_terms.سَهْم: Arrow — the hunting implement; its arrow's presence confirms the hunter killed the prey
key_terms.لَا بَأْسَ: No harm/no problem — standard jurisprudential formula permitting an action
key_terms.يَغِيبُ: It disappears (ghayyaba) — the animal vanishes from sight after being struck, introducing doubt about manner of death

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on eating game when one forgets to say bismillah while hunting, or the animal disappears after being shot?
ai.summary: Isa al-Qummi asked Imam al-Sadiq (AS) two questions about hunting with arrows. First, if one forgets whether they invoked the name of God (bismillah) before shooting, the Imam ruled the game is permissible to eat. Second, if the arrow struck an animal that then disappeared and was later found dead with the arrow in it, the Imam distinguished between the case where the carcass has not been partially eaten by another animal (permissible) and the case where it has been partly consumed (forbidden). This reflects the Shia jurisprudential principle that doubt does not override the presumption of permissibility in such cases, while partial consumption by another predator casts doubt on the manner of death.
